utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-R77.4, the Prosecutor versus Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We've come to the point where the Defence may present its case, where I do understand that Mr. Dieckmann says that he is not intending to call any witnesses. Is there any other evidence you would like to lead?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, perhaps he can make a decision on that after we've closed our case. I don't think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If you have an arrangement, then Mr. Dieckmann can still think about it during the presentation of your case, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's just -- of course, there is -- it gives him the option of calling evidence if he wishes, but I think that's the proper way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It could be the other way around as well, that you can consider to call any additional evidence which Mr. Dieckmann has not called. Are you ready to call your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence calls Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Haraqija, I think it's appropriate that you change place, and that you take the witness-stand, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll see that my client is on crutches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It wasn't a terribly serious accident, but it happened at the Detention Unit whilst he was playing volleyball. He has a torn ligament, and that's the reason for the crutches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we begin, Your Honours, just as a point of clarification, should the Prosecution understand now that Mr. Dieckmann may now be presenting evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, he has left that open; and, apparently, the order -- but, first, since Mr. Haraqija is on crutches, let's not wait. Mr. Haraqija, you are now in a different place in this courtroom. You are now a -- you will be a witness in your case. That means that you have to answer all the questions, and that's one of the consequences of your choice to appear as a witness in your own case. You'll have to give the solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and you'll be condition cross-examined by or at least the Prosecution has a possibility to cross-examine you. I take it that you've discussed this with counsel. I just wanted to make you perhaps, once again, aware of the situation you're in now. Before you give evidence, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher. Perhaps, I hope --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haraqija. Please be seated. Yes. Now, perhaps, I interrupted Mr. Saxon at the moment, apparently. Of course, the Chamber will follow the order agreed upon by the parties who is the first one to present its case. That means that Mr. Dieckmann, who has indicated already that he'll not call any witnesses, that he may want to tender other evidence, perhaps not through a witness. Mr. Saxon, is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would simply like to clarify whether Mr. Dieckmann intends to call any witnesses, including the accused Mr. Morina, because I've been given no notice of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that he will not call any witnesses. There are, of course, other ways to introduce evidence. Sometimes documentary evidence is introduced, for example, through the bar table. I don't know whether he has any plans to do so, but that apparently he reserves his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is exactly the understanding of my position now. From the very moment, we do not intend to present any witness, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Let me be clear. Two questions: Do you intend to call witnesses? I think it's fair that the Prosecution would know that at this moment. Another matter is whether there's any documentary evidence you would like to introduce in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: There is not in the moment, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But again and again, at this moment, I think after the Prosecution has concluded its case presentation, I think the Prosecution should be aware of whether you intend to call any witnesses. I mean, under normal circumstances, you would have to give your 65 ter list of witnesses, and you would need the approval of the Bench to add anything to your 65 ter list. So, at the end of the Prosecution's case, you should make up your mind as to whether you want to call any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We do not intend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do not intend to call any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, formally, if you would like to introduce any documentary evidence, you should include any exhibits on your exhibit list under 65 ter as well. That, however, might be less traumatic if you would later seek the approval of the Chamber to add any documents to your empty 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: For the sake of formality, could you just give your name to the Court for the record.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, as I explained before, two things particularly need to be remembered. The first is that throughout this questioning, you must remember to refer to the country we're talking about as the third country and a particular witness that we're talking about as Witness 2. You'll try to remember that, will you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And can I just check, the book you've got in front of you, is that blank or anything written inside it?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I have something written on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Are you just writing on blank pages at the moment?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I'm writing on a blank page, writing the questions you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, I just raise that so it's brought to the attention of the Judges and my learned friend for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see there's any harm in him making notes as long as he doesn't refer to any material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution doesn't object for the witness to make notes, but I would certainly agree with Mr. Khan, as long as he does not refer to any other written material in that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Or any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, the Chamber cannot see, as a matter of fact, your table. You are entitled to write, and that's even the best solution --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will remove the pages on which I had written something before. Now the notebook is blank, and there is nothing written on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Haraqija, this is not a race, but I do want to move on. We have an awful lot to try to cover today if we're going to conclude proceedings, which is the wish I think of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to lead on some background matters that I believe are not in dispute just to save time. If my friend takes objection, of course, I will desist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, is it correct that, on Monday, you started -- you gave some comments in an opening statement to the Trial Chamber and you fully adopt that statement whilst you are under oath now?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Upon your advice, I just wanted to introduce myself in the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, cutting straight to the relevant matters in this case, in 2005, you were a minister, were you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. From 4th of December, 2004, I was a minister of -- in the Ministry of Culture, Youth, and Sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And discussing some of the matters predating the allegations made by the Prosecution, is it correct that a lot of destruction of cultural property had taken place in Kosova in recent years?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the events of March 2004 had a great impact on the cultural heritage, the Orthodox culture heritage, which was a pity for the entire population of Kosova because these are values of the entire state of Kosova. Kosova doesn't have a sea, so that's why it should look after its cultural heritage. We have a lot of cultural heritage in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Were you particularly involved in the rebuilding of a church?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: After assuming the duty of the minister, my priority was to fulfil the pre-status demands, which included the cultural heritage, and at the same time the building of the opera house, Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, that was to be built in Pristina. After assuming this duty, in cooperation with UNMIK, we drafted a strategic plan on how to protect the cultural heritage. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Just one moment. The church belonged to which community?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: It was an Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that church, what state was it in when you found it, when you were first involved in the project?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Many services tried to present Kosova as a black sheep. These damages had not occurred only in Gjakova, but in many other cities in Kosova. That's why we wanted to deal with this issue through two phases, to rebuild them and to educate the coming generations, because the Kosovan people were used to the former Milosevic police to come out of these churches. These cultural heritage cannot be protected only through uniform but through civilians as well, and most of all when we know that Kosova's population is quite young.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did the church need rebuilding? Just try and answer the question. Did the church need rebuilding?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Of course, the church needed to be rebuilt as well as other facilities of historic value. In cooperation with UNMIK and the European Council --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Haraqija, but I know it's difficult. You have a lot to say, but I'm just trying to get the key points for Their Honours' attention. So I do apologise for interrupting. What state was the church in? Just very briefly. Was it in one piece or was it in a very bad state?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, sir, I cannot speak just of one church because it was not only just one church. We rebuilt a considerable number of churches, about 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, Mr. Khan did not ask you about the whole of the programme of rebuilding churches; he asked for one specific church. You should answer his questions. If he asks about one church, you should respond about that one church. What state was the church Mr. Khan was referring to and with which you had special involvement? What was the state of that church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a miserable state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, it's right, is it, that an example of this rebuilding was -- is shown on a DVD that your wife gave to the Defence team? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: As I said, this was done in two phases: Rebuilding the damaged facilities and, secondly, the education of the coming generations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you again. The question by Mr. Khan was whether the church he was talking about, whether you were given a DVD by your wife. Did you receive a DVD?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that DVD relates to the church rebuilding projects that you've just talked about, is that right, in a very small way?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at tab 7 on our 65 ter exhibit list -- sorry, on tab 8, you will see that there's an informational DVD. Your Honours, it's a few minutes. I don't intend to play it, but Your Honours are invited to look at it in due course and I would ask that it be given an exhibit number in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D3 is admitted into evidence; although not played, the Chamber will have a look at it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Bishop Pavle?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The head of the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you ever been in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: With the mediation of UNMIK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you met him?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: For which period of time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Belgrade in relation to the -- an attempt to forge closer ties and build bridges between the Serb and the ethnic Albanian communities? I'm talking about 2005.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I was there in 2005 in the capacity of minister of culture upon receiving an invitation from the Serbian minister of culture. My visit had to do with the restoration of the Orthodox facilities. This was the first visit of a Kosovan minister to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Haraqija, could you just tell the Court briefly how was that visit viewed amongst the Kosovan Albanian community in Kosova?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The Kosovan Albanian community did not evaluate it as a good visit, my visit to Belgrade, because they wanted me to focus my activities to Kosova. At the same time, the opposition at the time, due to the fact that there was nothing they could do to President Rugova and they knew that, I was a close associate of his, so they started a campaign against me, a media campaign. Every day we had different writings from the opposition appearing in the media against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I do apologise. And if this trip was going to be so unpopular in Kosova, why did you go ahead with it? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: It wasn't against the wish of Kosova people, but it was only some individuals who did not want this visit. In general, I come from Gjakova municipality. At that time, we had still 1.800 missing persons. Two days after my visit to Belgrade, I attended the funeral of two relatives of mine and Mr. Bardhyl Caushi. So it was not unpopular generally in Kosova but unpopular with some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That's very clear. Thank you. Now, you know that the Prosecution in this case have discussed your membership of a fund called the Defence Fund for Ramush Haradinaj. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I've been dealing with this issue for a year now and also with party issues. I know -- if I need to explain, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell the Court very briefly, why did you join that Defence Fund for Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I'm a member of the Democratic Alliance of Kosova, member of the Presidency. At the time, the late-President Rugova told me that I had to join this fund because the party led by the former Minister Haradinaj had a very small electorate, only 8 per cent; and at that time, our electorate was 45 per cent. So that's why he wanted me to join the fund and assist it, the Haradinaj fund, and in a way to assist the war, because you cannot equalise the victim with the offender. I accepted this and I mentioned in my opening statement Rugova was an inspiration. I admired him. So there was no chance that I would say no to any task he assigned me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Haraqija, is it correct that on the 3rd of April, 2007, you were interviewed by UNMIK in Kosova in relation to that fund?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you answer truthfully when you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Perhaps with the usher's assistance -- just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Could you look at this document, please. Is that your signature on the cover page of that document?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You can show him this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, I've got no idea what document we're talking about at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got copies for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you intend to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I do. I seek leave to add to the 65 ter list. It's simply to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't see it on your 65 ter list. Adding it to the 65 ter list, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Then leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, again to save time, if my learned colleague seeks to tender this document, I believe it's an interview the gentleman gave to UNMIK officials, so the Prosecution will not object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution will not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Haraqija, that being your interview -- well, that is your interview, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would ask that an exhibit number -- well, I would ask that leave be granted to add it to the 65 ter list and an exhibit number be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave was already granted to add it to the 65 ter list. There is -- Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D4 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course, you were not a member of the same party as Mr. Haradinaj, were you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you ever contested against the AAK, that being the party of Mr. Haradinaj, in political elections?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: To this date I contest this party, against this party. If you want me to explain, I can do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Please, briefly, if you could give the Court some examples of any political contests you've had with the AAK in Kosova and the outcomes.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Since 2000 and up to 2007, when the fifth election was held, I was the rival of Mr. Haradinaj. In the municipality I come from, the -- his base was there and we know that 1.800 men, young men from Gjakova, actively participated in the war of the UCK. In 2001 during the parliamentary election, in 2002, and in 2003 election, we opposed the AAK, including the 2004. So we opposed this party during the four elections. I was beaten by his party, nevertheless, in Gjakova during my candidacy for the president of -- mayor of this town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In what year were you beaten in the electoral contests?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: After I started to be questioned by the investigators of the OTP in 2007, I was successful during the first round in September, but I was beaten at the second round in December 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Were you ever successful against the AAK in the Gjakova municipality?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. We won the elections four times in Gjakova municipality, we won over AAK, which was our main rival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And by that, you mean you won, you won a seat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I was the president of the local self-government in Gjakova municipality. I led this institution for 21 months. Afterwards, I was appointed by President Rugova for minister of culture, and then I abandoned the former post. But as I said, I led this body for 21 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And just two more questions on this topic, just for the record, what years did you win these four elections in Gjakova against Ramush Haradinaj's party?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The first local elections were held in 2000, then the parliamentary election in 2001, then again local elections in 2002, parliamentary election in 2004; while in 2007, both local and parliamentary election was held, but we were beaten during this election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you say in response to the Prosecution allegation that your membership of the Haradinaj defence fund is evidence that somehow you are personally committed to Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Well, that is why the Prosecution -- that is what the Prosecution is paid for; however, it is a Trial Chamber that will decide whether I'm guilty or innocent. As I've already said, Ramush Haradinaj is my rival. I joined this fund because I was authorised to do this by President Rugova and because of the fact that many individuals accused the LDK and President Rugova of being collaborators with the Serbs in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And it's correct, is it, that you gave the same account to UNMIK investigators in April 2007 before these allegations were ever raised?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I cannot hide the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, did you ever ask Bajrush Morina to contact the protected witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you know the identity of the protected witness in this case in July 2007?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The first time I met Witness number 2 was here in the courtroom, and I didn't know that he was a witness. I read a statement of this Witness 2 in the media, but I didn't deal with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you ever plan to go to the third country we've been speaking about the last couple of days to speak to Witness 2?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Fortunately, thanks to my parents, I fulfilled all the plans; but in this case, I didn't have any plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. I think the translation sometimes is a bit ambiguous. Let me try and put it again. Did you ever plan to go to the third country to meet Witness 2?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you ever submit a travel request to go to the third country during this period?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I don't remember this, but usually it's not me who files these requests; it is the administration unit that does this part of the job.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I requested to go, then I would have gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, sometimes it's simpler, with the problem of translation we're having with Albanian, to answer yes or no wherever you can. I know it's not your fault, but let me try again. Did you ever request anybody to book you an aeroplane ticket to go to the third country we're talking about in this case, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you ever, directly or indirectly, threaten Witness 2 in this case?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No. All these fabrications on the part of the Prosecution and Witness 2, it's their problem, not me. It is very difficult for me to be here - not here in the witness-stand but there where the accused sits - it's a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Haraqija. Last question, and forgive me, I know your case, I'm doing it for the record for Their Honours. Did you ever seek to dissuade Witness 2 or any protected witness under the ICTY, dissuade them from testifying before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful. If you can stay there for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for once, I was within the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's appreciated, Mr. Khan. Mr. Dieckmann, would you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. Perhaps in my -- I still do have ten minutes actually of my allotted time, just two formal matters very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I take it you have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, and I apologise to Mr. Saxon. If the witness can be shown Prosecution exhibit under tab 11 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, you'll see there a travel request purporting to be dated the 6th of July, 2007, with manuscript writing at the bottom. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: As the witness said yesterday, it is her signature. I think it is the signature of the deputy minister, Angjelina Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you see at the top of that document the name of Mr. Mon Zhubi?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: He is - it's not in dispute - he's the permanent secretary, is that right, of the ministry? He was the permanent secretary of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes, he exercised that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If this request had been approved or had been formally submitted and approved, would any other signature have been on that document?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Usually, for my travels, the deputy minister dealt with this issue. It was not her who approved these travel requests. These were presented to the secretary and ultimately approved by the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So, in fact, you would expect the signature of Mon Zhubi to be on the document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's quite a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For chief, it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the evidence already before the Court; it's the evidence the witness gave -- Angjelina Krasniqi gave yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's not the evidence of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you refer to the evidence of Ms. Krasniqi, especially about what one would expect of signatures and by whom, then please point to it with great precision, so that we can check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, if you look at the document next to it, it's a trip of Mr. Morina to a third country. Can you see that document? It's the one without manuscript writing .

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you see anything next to the name of Mr. Mon Zhubi?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is any --

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The finance office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We should know exactly what document we are talking about at this moment. We also have to check with the witness whether he has -- you said the next document. The next for me is the one with last three digits ERN 285. Is that the document you're referring to in the original? Mr. Khan, we'd like to know exactly what document you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my file, it's the document -- well, it's Prosecution Exhibit 022, and I was led to believe it was under tab 11 as well. It's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are asking the witness to look at the document at tab 11. Now, tab 11 is a series, as admitted into evidence, is a series of travel documents. If you could tell us first in the original, because the witness is the first one to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the one with the ERN number at the top right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And I think it's perhaps the third or fourth from the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, the original in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original in Albanian, 297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got it. I've got it. Could someone check with the witness that he's got the right document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have the number here. Your Honours, I have the number here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you see Mr. Mon Zhubi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's check first. What is the number at the right top of the page you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0624-4297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll focus on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you see the name of Mr. Mon Zhubi typed at the top of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would give us one second to find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Khan, can you give us the English ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Your Honour, it is EDT. It has an EDT number 0624-4297, 0624-4297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is there a signature next to the name of Mr. Mon Zhubi?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Mon Zhubi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know what that signature at that location signifies?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: That means that the request has been approved, the request for travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And is that the manner in which requests are approved?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. In the Ministry of Culture, there were many travels at that time. The civil service was responsible for that, especially the secretary, she was responsible for this -- such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. If you can wait there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am grateful and I'm sorry if I handled it in a rather disorganized manner. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, apology is accepted. One additional question to the witness. Could you tell us whose handwriting and signature we find at the bottom of that same document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's the same signature, the bottom and top. It's only bigger and smaller, so that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the -- is there any text above the date, the date 6/7/7? 6/07/07, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the writing here. It's not very clear. It should say here "approved."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Mr. Saxon, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My name is Dan Saxon. I'm originally from the city of Boston in the United States and I represent the Office of the Prosecutor in these proceedings, and I've got some questions for you this morning. I understood from your responses to the questions of my learned friend Mr. Khan that you deny all of the allegations that the Prosecution has made against you in this case; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So, then, I'd just like to go back for a moment. When you were serving as the minister of culture, youth, and sport, you were responsible for the work of that ministry; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that would mean also you were responsible for the work of the employees of that ministry; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I'm responsible for the ministry, not for the employees. The employees are responsible for themselves. This is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that I understand your position, you say the employees are responsible for themselves. Is it your position that you, as the minister, would have no responsibility at all for the conduct of the employees of that ministry?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: For the behaviour of the employees, we have the disciplinary committees, different committees, which we had in the ministry. I can submit written complaints or oral complaints, but there are committees in the ministry. The civil service is unseparated from the political component.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But you would also agree with me that, as the minister, you were responsible for the work -- for the quality of the work performed by the employees of the ministry; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This is normal because the vote of the people is very important, so the vote of the people can take you forward or can take you backward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So going back to the fact that you deny all of the Prosecution's allegations in this case, just so that I understand your position then, it's your position that Mr. Morina went to visit Witness 2 in the third country in July of 2007 strictly on his own accord; that is, for Mr. Morina's personal, private reasons? That's your position, right?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: We have been dealing with this issue for one year now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I stick to what I've already said about this visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I need an answer to my question, sir. Can you answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Bajrush Morina went there on his own. He did not go at my own request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And, so, it's also your position, then, that you had absolutely nothing to do with the meetings between Mr. Morina and Witness 2 that occurred in the third country in July of 2007; right?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I had nothing, absolutely nothing, to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So continuing, then, logically, it's also your position that when Mr. Morina told Witness 2 and investigators of this Tribunal that you had directed Mr. Morina to meet with Witness 2, that was a complete fabrication; right? That's your position, isn't it? Mr. Morina is making all of this up in terms of your involvement?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that he had fabricated such things. But the co-accused, I believe he is also the victim of the game of Witness 2 in cooperation with the Prosecutors, as you have already failed in other processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let's take this a little bit more slowly then. First of all, you don't believe that Mr. Morina was lying when he implicated you in the events of this case; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do wonder if this is proper cross-examination. He is putting, asking the client to comment on the evidence of a completely different person. He must -- proper cross-examination is ask the witness to confront his account, which is completely denying this case, or to confront him with evidence. But to ask him to guess and second-guess what Mr. Morina said and why he said it is not proper cross-examination in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is evidence about statements, there's evidence about the events in the third country, statements have been given explaining what had happened. The witness may be confronted with that evidence. So, Mr. Saxon, if you would do that. If you would put to him that during the conversation and in the statement, the conversation between Morina and the witness and the statement given by Mr. Morina, that he talks about the involvement of the present witness, you may put that to the witness and ask the witness whether that is untrue, whether that is fabricated or a lie. Perhaps you have understood meanwhile what the question is, Mr. Haraqija. Was Mr. Morina, when he gave his statement and when he had a recorded conversation with the witness, was he not speaking the truth when he said that he acted on your instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stick to what I already said. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said Mr. Morina did not tell the truth --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not during this conversation and also not when he gave his statement as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If Mr. Morina, then, was not telling the truth, if he was making this up, then logically Mr. Morina would do that to place responsibility on you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is completely inappropriate. A cross-examining party can't ask a witness to speculate as to the motives of another individual. He should confront him with evidence, put forward any other evidence he wants to the accused to controvert his denial. But to ask him to speculate as to somebody else's intention is ludicrous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is there any basis on which you could expect this witness to know about the motives of what other people did; and if so, please lay that foundation and then ask the question. If not, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to play a portion of the interview of Mr. Morina with OTP investigators. This is now Exhibit P19. And the portion that will be played in the transcript, in the English transcript, will be page 24, line 29, to page 25, line 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we find it in the binder, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tab 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for those following in the Albanian language, this is at page 21. This clip will begin at page 21, line 36, to page 22, line 5. And the time code for this audio-recording is two hours, three minutes to -- excuse me, two hours, three minutes, and two seconds to two hours, five minutes, and 50 seconds. If that clip could now be played right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours. Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask Mr. Saxon in what tab is the Albanian language because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's tab 8 after the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Haraqija, you're going to be able to hear this. You're going to be able to listen to the words, and you're also going to be able to see the words in your own language on the screen in front of you, all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that disappears as soon as it's been played. I'm wondering what the advantages of listening to it rather than to read it, which gives a good focus on the words spoken. And Mr. Haraqija, I take it, from his --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the meantime, I wonder if the usher could help my client find the right tab, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please tab 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Tab 8, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if Mr. Haraqija's binder could be turned to page 21 of the Albanian version, and if this cannot be published to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Haraqija, starting at line 36 [sic] on that page, you'll see a question beginning with: "And you have, in fact, called Haraqija after the first meeting ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to continue. I'm going to use the word "Witness 2" instead of the name of the witness. "That's what you told" Witness 2? "Just for ease of reference, page 3, 3 out of 44, on the second day. Witness 2 "asked you, 'Maybe, maybe it will happen. Did Astrit call you? What did he say?' Then you respond: 'No, he didn't either. I called him yesterday ...'" Now on page 25 of the English version. "He sent me a message later. 'I told you, man. I said I stayed with this man,' he said ... And then apparently he decided not to come. Do you remember it now?" You've been following me, Mr. Haraqija?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Saxon, that where you said, "Then you respond ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The questioner is speaking to Mr. Morina during this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And now continuing on page 25, line 4 of the English, Mr. Morina responds in the following: "I don't remember exactly; but as far as I remember, I spoke with Veli Bytyqi because I wasn't able to contact the Minister, because, as far as I remember, the Minister at that time was in Brussels. I said to" Witness 2 "like this, instead of going into the matter of who is Veli Bytyqi, because just to cut matters short, I might have said that I spoke to the Minister, but in fact, it was - I spoke to his spokesman. In other words, I didn't really lie all that much. I said that I spoke to the Minister, in fact I spoke to his spokesperson. And I took what the spokesperson said, his message, his instructions, as being word of the Minister. I didn't reach the Minister. I think that I've tried to, but I'm very sure that I didn't." Have you been following me, Mr. Haraqija?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, in this passage, Mr. Morina is effectively, as he puts it -- he's saying: "I didn't really lie all that much," but he is effectively correcting a lie, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: As I already said earlier, I don't want to attack my co-accused because he's a victim, a victim of the game of the Prosecutors and of Witness Number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you are asking the witness to interpret and to explain a portion of an interview in which he did not take part, and what Mr. Morina is telling in this interview to those who are interviewing him, is there any reason to believe that the witness could better interpret that than the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to put it to you, Mr. Haraqija, that you directed Mr. Morina to meet with Witness Number 2 for two reasons: In order to convince the witness not to testify against Mr. Haradinaj; and, two, to facilitate a meeting between yourself and Witness 2. Do you want to respond to what I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: It's your right to say what you want because that's what you are paid for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will take that as your response. Mr. Haraqija, in 2007, you had a deputy minister working for you named Angjelina Krasniqi; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if the witness could be assisted now, I would like to turn to tab 7 in that binder. This is now Exhibit P18. Actually, I'm going to move on. I'm going to move on, and I'm not going to refer to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you about travel authorisations within the ministry. Mr. Haraqija, when you were the minister of culture, you often authorised employees of the ministry to travel abroad, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The purpose of the Ministry of Culture, Youth, and Sport has been also to internationalise sports and to establish links with the Albanian Diaspora because there are many, many Albanians who live outside of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question simply was whether you often authorised employees to travel abroad. Did you often do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, indeed, given all of the travelling that ministry employees had to do, sometimes you directed staff members to travel to certain events, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No. Without invitation, they could not go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Haraqija, let's take the situations where invitations had arrived to the Ministry of Culture. When there were such invitations to an event in third countries, sometimes you would direct particular staff members to travel to participate in those events, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You never once as minister, after the ministry received a particular invitation, directed a particular employee to travel and participate in an event? You never did that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I said when there are special invitations, especially -- we were especially engaged at the time in efforts to set up legal infrastructure of the ministry. We had to harmonize all the laws with the international community, especially with the Council of Europe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question. The question simply was whether, when there was an invitation, whether you ever directed a particular employee to travel and participate in an event. Did you ever say to someone upon having received an invitation, I would like you to go there to that event for which we received an invitation? Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but I have to be clear in -- as far as the question is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said people could not travel if there was no invitation. When there was an invitation, did you ever say to one of the employees of the ministry, I'd like you to go there and attend the event for which we are invited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say there has been an issue even from the opening statement regarding translation. Just as a point, I think if my learned friend has problem with one question, I think rephrasing it, as Your Honour just did now, is a very helpful way of overcoming the translation problems from Albanian that we've been having.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in fact, you also had the authority to direct your employees not to travel to a particular event, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Generally, I had the authority to stop anybody from going abroad when I thought that they should not travel abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to show you, please, part of the interview that my office did with Mr. Morina on the 26th of October, 2007 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, before I do that, if we could show the witness tab 11, please. Your Honours, this is now P22. And I'm aware that there are a number of pages, and I would direct the parties' attention to what is ERN 0624 to 4292. And if we could move into private session for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that I understand your position, Mr. Haraqija, did you ever approve a request of Mr. Morina to travel for personal reasons? Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The requests and the invitations -- and there are, in fact, hundreds of invitations and requests coming to the Ministry of Culture, Youth, and Sport, and I do not think that I saw that Bajrush Morina was travelling for the first time. For as long as he was there, he must have travelled a lot of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But it wasn't appropriate for employees of the ministry to travel using ministry funds for personal reasons, was it?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I do not think he travelled for persons reasons. You see here that there is an invitation, so he must have travelled in order to go there upon this invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now -- if we can move into public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah, that is correct, Your Honour. Thank you. If we can -- Mr. Usher, if you could help the witness, please, and if we could turn to what is tab 8. It's Exhibit P19. And for those following along in English, if you could turn to page 13, line 29. And if the usher could help Mr. Haraqija, please, turn to page 12, where we will start at line 11 in the Albanian version. And I do think I need to move into private session again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that that was a legitimate invitation, to meet with members of the so-called Albanian Diaspora in that city?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a foundation should be laid. The witness said he's never seen this document before. He should firstly be asked -- well, Your Honour, it's quite basic. I think Your Honour will carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, first of all, what is a legitimate invitation? I'm in doubt as to what that exactly means --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the witness has told us that he sees this document for the first time. Was that first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it here for the first time. As I said, I have received many invitations when I was minister of culture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never discussed it with your counsel, this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have discussed, yes, but we did not discuss on this invitation. This is the first time I saw this invitation, when I came here. As I told you, we received thousands of invitations in the Ministry of Culture. I cannot remember each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But this invitation plays a prominent role in these proceedings; at least it plays a role. You never discussed the content of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's lawyer/client privilege. That's completely inappropriate in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the witness tells us today that he sees something today for the first time, and I think I'm entitled to ask the witness whether he had knowledge - and that's what I'm asking now the content - whether he has knowledge of this document. He has taken the stand, and that's is own choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what is relevant -- first, every question must be relevant. What is relevant is did he see this document prior to his indictment by the Prosecution. But the way I prepare my case with my client and what documents I showed to my client and what lays behind it is a matter, with the greatest of respect, which the Chamber should not enter upon and is trespassing, in fact. It's covered by legal professional privilege --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Legal professional privilege imposes a duty on counsel not to say anything about what he learned from confidential conversations with his client. That privilege for counsel is also just as valid as a client still imposes this duty on counsel. It's entirely in the hands of the client whether or not to give any information. I'll discuss this matter of a legal nature over the break with my colleagues, and then see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honour, the point is, of course, the privilege attaches to the client not to the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The privilege attaches to the client, but he can't be compelled to start answering questions about the communications he's had with his counsel. It's, in my submission, it's a compelling point, but Your Honours will perhaps consider it over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it over the break. Mr. Saxon, further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you wish to take the break now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd also like to know from you how much time you think you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I believe I need about another 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, the Chamber has considered the way in which you used your time until now, and the Chamber grants ten minutes after the break to conclude your cross-examination. We have a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity to continue, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Khan, I have heard your objection against the question. We have considered the matter during the break in quite some depth. We expect you not to intervene any more at this moment. We have heard your objection, and I will put one or more questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, we're talking earlier about the documents, the invitation. You told us that you have seen this document for the first time today. My question to you is: Did you never see this document or discuss with anyone, including Mr. Khan, the content of this document which is the invitation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sincerely said that I saw this document here because this issue became a case, but this does not mean that I haven't seen it in Pristina due to the reasons that in our office we received many invitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about this invitation, and the question is two-fold: First, whether you've seen it before today; second, whether you discussed the content of it with anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible to have seen the invitation in Pristina but not paid attention to it because there were many invitations. I saw it here, but I did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not discuss it with anyone before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You gave now two answers. The first one that you did not discuss it. Now you say: "I don't remember."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said, I had received many invitations in the past while I was in Kosova. This one may be part of those invitations that I've seen. However, the content of this invitation, I did not discuss it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not with anyone, including in your conversations with Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall to have discussed it with Mr. Khan because, as I said at the opening of this trial, I don't feel comfortable in the position of the accused. I feel under stress. I don't remember all the details in this story, but I don't think I have discussed it with Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, as a minister -- as the minister of culture, you must have kept a very busy schedule; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: It depends on the period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you met with high-level officials, didn't you, ambassadors, foreign ministers?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I met with ambassadors, with presidents, with ministers of different countries of south-eastern Europe, with foreign secretaries, including the foreign secretary of the United States, of England, with their departments for foreign affairs. I've met with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, on a typical working week between Monday and Friday, you would have had a busy schedule, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: As I said, it depended on the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you a document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance can we turn to what is tab 27. Your Honours, that would be in your second binder. And if the witness could be assisted, please, and if we could turn to the Albanian version. Your Honours, in the English version, we will focus on the first page as ERN number 0624-4331. In the Albanian version, we will focus on the third page, which has the same ERN number, 0624-4331.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, this is a copy of your agenda from April through July 2007. It was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor pursuant to a search warrant issued by the Trial Chamber, and this copy was obtained by investigators on the 8th of November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been produced as part of the witness statement of Peter Mitford-Burgess or as an associated document with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can please turn your mind, Mr. Haraqija, to the entry for Tuesday, the 10th of July; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, perhaps you could assist the witness. It is the third page in the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see Tuesday, July 10th?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you see on Tuesday that day, the 10th of July, you have an appointment from noon to 12.30, do you see that, a meeting with a karate player?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then we see after 12.30, on the 10th of July, you have no commitments until 9.30 in the morning on the 12th of July. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Well, this does not mean that all my meetings -- there were entries for all my meetings in the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, but the purpose of keeping an agenda is to record what your commitments are so that you can keep them, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: We were not duty-bound to put them on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, you were completely free on the 11th of July, Wednesday, a working day, do you see that, according to this agenda?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I don't think it includes all my commitment. Usually, on Wednesdays at 12.00, I have meetings with members of the LDK. That's why I was quite surprised not to see this entry for a meeting with the LDK because we had party meetings twice a week. So these were meetings of the LDK at central level. So as the -- in the position of the chairman of Gjakova municipality, I had to participate in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, can you turn the page, please. On the next page, you will see Wednesday, June 27th. We're going back in time now. And you will see that there is no entry for a meeting at 12.00 with members of your party, is there?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: That's what I, in fact, said, that the agenda does not contain all the entries. You can go through the minutes of the meetings of the LDK central committee, and you will see there that I attended every meeting. On Wednesdays and Mondays in Pristina, we hold meetings of the leadership of the LDK. These meetings were -- are also held in Gjakova for technical reasons sometimes; and in these meetings, I also participate once a week. If it was impossible for me to travel to Gjakova, then I would hold these meetings of the LDK party in Pristina twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, I would like to put it to you that you kept Wednesday, the 11th of July, free on your calendar in case that you decided finally to travel to the third country to meet with Witness 2. How would you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I don't think your question has a good foundation. You see the entry for 18th June, that part, in that section there's no entry. I'm just following your example, Mr. Prosecutor. You see for the dates 14th and 15th May. There is no entry either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I limited your time. One or two or three short questions. I mean, it was a ruling by the Chamber that you would have ten minutes. You have now taken those ten minutes approximately, so, therefore, take our ruling seriously. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, you believed -- I'll start again. You agreed to become the deputy chairman of the committee to defend Ramush Haradinaj in part because you believed that the prosecution of Ramush Haradinaj by this Tribunal was unjust, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No, this is not what I said. With the request of the late-president, Mr. Ibrahim Rugova, I became the deputy chairman for raising funds for Haradinaj. As I said earlier, there were individuals at the time who claimed that President Rugova was a Serb collaborator and did not support the war. I have stated publicly in the media on frequent occasions that the parties that came out from the war do not have members as much as the LDK have fighters. I've already stated one of the reasons was that the AAK at the time only enjoyed 8 per cent of the electorate. At the time we were, as a party, were in coalition with this party. As we were --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, I have the following question for you. You twice during your testimony said that Witness 2 was -- let me just check so that I can quote you literally. You told us that you believed Mr. Morina also to be the victim of the game of Witness 2 in cooperation with the Prosecutors. Could you explain to us what that game was and how Mr. Morina became a victim in this game.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I still think -- after everything that I've read, I'm fully convinced that the co-accused is a good man. He comes and has a wonderful family. I don't know the intentions of Witness 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you not to explain about the family of Witness 2. I asked you what was the game that was played, as you suggested, by Witness 2 in cooperation with the Prosecutors? Let's first leave it to that. What was the game?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Most sincerely, Your Honour, I think that this is the game of Witness 2, either for his personal interest or because he's paid by someone, because Witness 2, as we understand now, was a witness in the Haradinaj trial. I don't know his personal profit and why he blemished my name and the name of Mr. Morina. It is Witness 2 who knows this best. You, as a Trial Chamber, will decide on this, but I deny all the allegations that the Prosecution made against me, and I'm proud of my name as Astrit Haraqija. Maybe I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are giving speeches rather than answer my questions. A game suggests, if it's a game, as you said, between Witness 2 and the Prosecution, that two people are in one way or the other engaged in that game. Now, tell us what that game was.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: In my opinion, it is a game because they share the same aim: To blemish the good names in Kosova. As they failed in the Haradinaj trial, the Prosecutor had to come up with something else, which again was unfounded. And that's why I said that Mr. Morina was a victim of this game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how became he victimised? Because your answer suggests that they took Mr. Morina to the third country, or I do not see exactly how he became a victim.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I sincerely didn't deal with this issue. Now it's been ten months that I've been involved in this process, but the Prosecutor with the associates know very well how they organized this game. Mr. Morina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Being a victim suggests that something happens to you that you do not want. I would like you to explain to me at what moment something happened to Mr. Morina he wished not to happen, because that's what would make him a victim. When for the first time something happened Mr. Morina would not have wished to happen, where he was put in that situation by Witness 2 and the Office of the Prosecution. That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Maybe I'm being misunderstood. I'm frankly saying that Mr. Morina, as it was proved by Witness 2, had previous meetings with him. They had different interviews. In addition, Witness 2 was Witness 77, as I heard it here, in the Haradinaj trial. And this game, as I said, was prepared by Witness 2 for his personal gains in cooperation with the Prosecution. I don't know what their maths was, but they were involved in this game. I feel innocent and I believe Mr. Morina is also innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any fact known to you which could illustrate that the Office of the Prosecution was involved in whatever way with Mr. Morina's travel to the third country?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: The fact is the following. Why had Mr. Morina to go there on my behalf? I'm not a small child. I know who I am. I would have gone there myself. I wouldn't have needed to send Mr. Morina there. Maybe I'm not a hero but also I don't fear anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any fact known to you which could illustrate that the Office of the Prosecution influenced the conversation between Mr. Morina and Witness 2, wherein he said that he came, acted on your instructions, and that part of the conversation was about whether or not to testify? So is there any fact known to you that the Office of the Prosecution would have influenced the text spoken by Mr. Morina during this conversation with Witness 2?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: One of the facts is the indictment; secondly, it's not a good feeling to go in an investigation room and be locked there for hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood my question. I was referring to the conversation in the lobby of a hotel in the third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sat down very quietly; and, of course, it's for Your Honours to decide how to ensure a fair trial. But the witness at no stage has said that the Prosecution have put words, have -- how was it phrased? That he has not influenced the text spoken by Mr. Morina. That evidence has been given by Your Honour, with the greatest of respect. It has never come out of the mouth of my client. Your Honours, of course, it's an imperillous position for counsel to address the Bench when the Bench have sovereign discretion; but, Your Honour, there's no foundation at all for the question you've just put to the witness. The foundation, of course, only was the witness's view that he was part of a game because he had been unfairly indicted. Your Honour, I just put that down for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm exploring at this moment what is the basis for calling this a game, and I'm focusing very much on the time-line. Mr. Haraqija, you may have misunderstood the question, my question about whether in any way the Prosecution would have influenced the words spoken by Mr. Morina. I referred to the words spoken as recorded during the conversation with Witness 2 in the third country.

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I never worked for the Prosecution, and that's why I don't know how this game came to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. One other question. I have looked at your agenda, and you just looked at it as well, under tab 27. Now, this agenda, is this an agenda which is a hard-copy agenda, or is it a computerized agenda of which you can make print-outs?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the agenda was kept by my assistants. I had four assistants working in the Ministry of Culture, and they kept agenda concerning the official invitations for meetings. As for my personal agenda, I didn't keep it in the computer because, as I said, there were meetings at a party level on Mondays, on Wednesdays. I never made entries, so these meetings were afterwards. The entries for these meetings were updated and put into the computer by the assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you keep your personal agenda? Was this handwritten, hard copy? How did you keep that agenda?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Usually on my mobile phone, on the calendar and reminder section. On my private phone I kept these entries; for example, set a reminder for a meeting with deputy prime minister or meeting with family. So all these things, I kept it on my phone and set a reminder for them.
