utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you synchronise that with your assistants? Because if I try to imagine two different electronic agendas, one part of your agenda, the other another part of your agenda. How did you synchronise that with your assistants?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I was able to see the agenda. Let's say I received it on Monday morning for the entire week. In the meantime, we could have received other invitations. The meetings that I deemed unnecessary, I didn't participate at these meetings. For example, 16th of July, invitation by the International Northern Faculty, I didn't attend this meeting. Another example, there are plenty of examples here, invitation, 8.30 to 9.00, concert on the occasion of the visit of a mayor of a municipality, I didn't participate in this meeting. It doesn't mean that I took part in all the meetings. I took part only in those that I deemed important and necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Saxon, in the binder, as far as the agenda is concerned, I find many weeks covered in the original language. I see only two weeks covered in English. Now, the witness starts explaining more about the remainder of his agenda. For example, 16th of July doesn't appear in translation, so I have difficulties to fully understand without having received the translation. The witness has told us about his usual meetings at 12.00 on Wednesday. I still can decipher that most of the Wednesdays do not contain a 12.00 appointment, but what is there I cannot tell you without a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] With the greatest respect, Your Honour, Monday, July 16th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise. JUDGE ORIE. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But, yes, Your Honour, these -- with the resources, the translation resources that the Prosecution has, these were the pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, the 16th does not appear in English under tab 27. I have got two pages, the first one July 9th to July 15th --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the second one July the 2nd to July the 8th, and not July the 16th, which, of course, appears in the original but not in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are under a duty to provide translations of every exhibit. Would you please take care that the Chamber receives the whole of the agenda translated. Mr. Khan, you or I take it that at least the accused could read it, where the Chamber is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, no objection for a translation to be served after the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Also no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Khan, any need for further questions triggered either by the cross-examining party or by the questions put by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, were matters of your personal phone, were matters included on your daily planner that were not included on the schedule that's before you? Were appointments included on your mobile phone that cropped up that would not have been included on your personal planner; is that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: It is possible, of course. Only, if you look at the agenda, you will see that for some dates you have no entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, is it correct - this arises out of the Trial Chamber's questions of you - is it correct that I met you in Kosova between the 29th of May and the 1st of June of this year? Do you remember that, when I came alone or about that period, if you don't remember the dates, around that period?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes, we did meet, I know that, but I don't know the exact dates when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that's the only time I went to Kosova, is that right, in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: My two legal assistants, pro bono legal assistant, Caroline Buisman and Gissou Azarnia, who are sitting behind me, they came to Kosova, did they, between the 17th of July and the 24th of July. Do you remember that or thereabouts? I don't expect you to remember the exact dates, but do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that any documents -- they discussed with you various documents about this case?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that once they left, we were sending -- my team was sending to you confidentially by e-mail further batches of Prosecution disclosure that were received after that time to your private e-mail account? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes. You sent these materials, but I didn't look through all of them because I have problems with English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did we have an investigator in Kosova to assist your defence, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me put it again. Apart from Caroline Buisman and Gissou Azarnia, was anybody appointed by the Tribunal as an investigator that could conduct investigations, or was it done by Ms. Buisman and Ms. Azarnia?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: These two ladies and the interpreter who facilitated the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you open any of the e-mails that we sent you to your private account or not, or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: I opened some of them, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The invitation, did I ever produce that invitation to you and show it to you directly?

utterances.speaker: ASTRIT HARAQIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. I've got no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Haraqija, this concludes your testimony. I invite you take your old position again; that is, the position of an accused. Mr. Khan, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am. Before I do that, I'm very happy to call one of my legal assistants. Before I do that, I asked my learned friend before the break to agree a stipulation that we received the invitation that Your Honour was talking about for the first time in The Hague in a CD in our locker on the 21st of July, that's the date of the disclosure, 21st of July, when my Legal officer -- my legal assistant -- my pro bono assistant, because there was no funding, and the legal assistant, were already on the ground in Kosova. I'd like that stipulation, that that was the date this invitation was first given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just check one thing. I am checking the confirmation material which would have been provided to the Defence much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time for that. Meanwhile, Mr. Khan, we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you want, I'm very happy to call my legal assistant on this issue if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber is not calling any Chamber witnesses at this moment, so, therefore, if you want to do it, you should seek permission to add the witness to the 65 ter list, but Mr. Saxon apparently has found something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This invitation was contained within the confirmation material for this case, which, actually, was provided to the Defence, I believe, at the time of the initial appearance at the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hadn't seen it before, but that's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not attach great relevance to the fact whether the 21st of July or in the confirmation material you first received --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only matter I will raise, and my learned friend can dispute it - I raise it just because it's rather awkward because I don't want to give evidence myself; that's the difficulty of this inquiry - but I did inform the Prosecution that the first CD they gave which was given to the locker, which is not my locker, it is the locker of the Stojic team, I didn't receive that, and I sent an e-mail that I didn't receive that CD. Your Honour, I don't wish to belabour the point. Your Honour, another matter, I'm told by the legal assistant of the second accused that that invitation wasn't in their bundles either. It was served at court by Mr. Re in hard copy form. Your Honour, if you want to litigate it further, we can; but, otherwise, I am not going to go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not expressed any wish to further litigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness in that case is Edmond Kuqi, if he can be brought in. While he is brought in, if I could quickly summarize, with Your Honours' leave, the general areas of his testimony. He was the driver of Astrit Haraqija, and he drove my client's wife Zana to Peja for the opening of a theatre and he was present at the time. His evidence in his statement is that he heard no mention of the protected witness in this case, he heard no mention of ICTY proceedings or any order, as alleged by the Prosecution, to direct Mr. Morina to intimidate or harass or dissuade that witness from testifying. Your Honours, in addition, he will tender photographs which are detailed in the statement and in a separable part of the statement, detailing where people are sitting. Your Honours, I believe those have been distributed. No. Perhaps they can be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeing them. That concludes your summary, Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kuqi. Mr. Kuqi, before you give evidence, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Mr. Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Khan, who's counsel for Mr. Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you give your full name to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Edmond Kuqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And your date of birth is the 5th of August, 1971; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps, with the usher's assistance, the witness can be shown the statement dated the 19th of July in Albanian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kuqi, if you could please look at the -- this document. Is that a true record of a statement you gave on the 19th of July, 2008?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you've had the opportunity of reading that statement and verifying its contents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that if you were to give live evidence before the Court, you would attest all these matters as true? You would give evidence consistent with this statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In the statement, you mention indicating seating arrangements on two photographs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, perhaps the witness can be shown the two photographs in question and copies given to the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, these were shown previously to the Prosecution. They are on a separable part of the statement, and I would ask, with Your Honours' leave, if they could be added to the 65 ter list and given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, two requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please assign numbers to the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, photograph number 4D becomes Exhibit D5; and photograph 5D becomes Exhibit Number D6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D5 and 6, with the absence of objections, are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: These two photographs, what do they show? Could you deal with the one on your left first -- sorry, the one on your right, first, which is D6 -- sorry, it should be D5. I do apologise -- no, it's D6. Yes. If you could perhaps start with that one, what does that show?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: This is the place where we were sitting on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Where was that, which place?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: This is called Hotel Metohija in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Centre of which town?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the other photograph, what does that show, the one with many tables? There's four tables, and then at a right angle the tables continue with wicker chairs.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: This is the place where I went to after the performance. In the evening, we went there all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And have you indicated where various people are sitting on these photographs?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I have already shown you the place where the people were sitting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will leave it there. Any further clarification can be sought by the Prosecution with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I'd like to check is I see markings there. "Ast" stands for Astrit Haraqija?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to the right of that, yes. Of course, I'm not seeking or eliciting evidence from you, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: On the left of -- looking at the photograph, looking at the photograph, you see "Ast" in the middle. Is it correct that's Astrit Haraqija that is signified?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, again --

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: -- this is the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- and to the right, it says "Ast - wife." Is that Astrit Haraqija's wife?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, again, looking at the photograph to the left of Astrit, what name is there?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Kasapolli, Mr. Kasapolli.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And right at the top end of the table on the right, there is "E-d-i, Edi." Who is that?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And this document, D5, this is the photograph that you say shows the cafe in Peja; is that right, so we're clear?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And turning to the next photograph, the one that you say is the dinner that you went to after the performance, could you similarly assist the Trial Chamber by telling them what your abbreviations show. Who are the people detailed by the abbreviations? The first we come to on the right, it says "Ast.w." Who is that?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: His wife, Astrit's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: After that, it says "Ast." Is that Astrit Haraqija?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, Astrit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: After that?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Kasapolli.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And in the right and the left-hand side corner, there are two other names there that are rather difficult to read in the copy. Could you tell Their Honours what you've written there in those seating places?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Mr. Bytyqi and Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the other people, who were occupying the other chairs that you haven't put names on? Were they empty or were people sitting in them?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No, all the chairs were occupied. They were the actors who had performed on that night. They were also people of institutions from Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless you think I can take it further, I intend to leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to hear from the witness who was seated on the half-visible chair, bottom left, in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see that, Mr. Kuqi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Bytyqi, Veli Bytyqi, was sitting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And on the extreme right, if I didn't cover it before, the extreme right of the photograph, of D5, the cafe?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the first -- oh, yes. I see a slight red marking on the first chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: What do those red marks signify? You see, His Honour has drawn our attention to the red marks between where you say Veli is sitting and where the word "Bajrush" is annotated, and there are two red lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking of that line. It's just where he says the seat of Mr. Morina was, that is, because it is almost impossible to read it. That's the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- chair right-hand side row. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bajrush is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And is anything signified by those two lines or not?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: They were very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Close --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as far as the lines are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If you could stay there, there will be some questions from my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Mr. Dieckmann, do you have any questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Kuqi, it's now afternoon, so good afternoon. My name is Dan Saxon. I represent the Prosecution in this case. I'm from the United States. You were the driver of Mr. Haraqija in the summer of 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in your statement, you talk about this social cultural event that you drove him to in the city of Peja. How often would or how often did you take Mr. Haraqija to similar kinds of social cultural events? Once a week? More? Less? How often?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Whenever that was necessary, whenever there were invitations, whenever he asked me, I took him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure. But can you give us a general estimate. Were invitations given to him on a weekly basis?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how many months did you serve as his driver?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Officially, six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Six years. Would it be fair to say that during those six years that you drove and accompanied Mr. Haraqija to these kinds of social or cultural events dozens of times?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I have been his driver from the morning until late whenever he wanted me to stay with him. Whenever he wanted me to take him somewhere, I took him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Kuqi, I don't know if there's a problem with the translation. I thought my question was fairly simple. You told us that you served as Mr. Haraqija's driver for six years, so my question was: Would it be fair to say that during those six years, you would have accompanied Mr. Haraqija to such -- these kinds of social gathering dozens of times over those six years?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this gathering, this evening in Peja, first at the cafe and then the dinner party after the theatre, that was a typical social cultural gathering like many others that you had attended; right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as you describe in your statement, the conversations were generally light-hearted; right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, please, for those other dozens of social gatherings to which you accompanied Mr. Haraqija, are you able to tell the Trial Chamber the seating positions of the persons who were present?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: It depends on the event. It depends on the events. You asked me about that particular event, and I described it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to understand. You acknowledged that this was a typical social gathering; right? And I'm just trying to understand, was there something special about this event that stuck in your memory or permitted you to keep the seating arrangements stuck into your memory?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No, there was nothing special; the usual thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can show the witness what I believe is now Exhibit D5, it's the photograph -- or if the witness can take a look at the photograph where -- of the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You have that -- you can see that photograph now?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you see -- actually, before I ask you some questions about this photograph, during this gathering at the cafe, did anyone go up -- get up to use the restroom?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you taking note of this, though?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I did not stay in the cafe for a long time. We just had a cup of coffee and then we went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you look in this photograph, you see two motor-scooters there in the upper left-hand counter. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, whether those motor-scooters were there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: These photos have been taken lately. There was a vehicle in the place of the motor-scooters, and there was another car then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see some people walking by here. Were there people passing by, walking by, that evening?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, definitely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, occasionally, did you observe these people?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, how are you able to tell us, then, that there were persons walking by?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: It was day; and, of course, I saw people passing before me just -- my eyes must have been in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Moving toward -- toward the dinner after the theatre, which would be where you have the seating arrangement in D6, you were sitting a bit outside of this picture, is that correct, a bit to what we see -- a bit off the left edge of this photograph? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How far away were you from that table?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Not very far away. This was a table in which four people were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you able to hear every single conversation that took place around these tables?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, then, you cannot be sure then that during that evening, after the theatre, someone might have mentioned the case of Mr. Haradinaj, can you?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: It's clear in the photo that I was sitting close to Mr. Haraqija, his wife, and Mr. Kasapolli. There were also the municipal officials and also the theatre actors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But you were not able to hear every single conversation around that table, could you?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So it is at least possible then, isn't it, that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say, as I said for the last -- for the witness yesterday, we're not alleging any of these witnesses, including the next one, is omniscient, and that definitively certain things were not discussed. All they can say is that they heard certain things. I hope that's, to a degree, of assistance to my learned friend. I is not being alleged; it's definitive. It's simply the people who were present, that we're calling, didn't hear anything of that nature. I don't think a witness can't be expected to say more. I don't know whether it helps or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it helps or not, you've said it now, Mr. Saxon heard it, and he's invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At the dinner, you mentioned that there were around 40 people present?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It must have, then, gotten fairly loud in this room during the dinner?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And wouldn't all of that other conversation going on have possibly prevented you from hearing bits of a conversation that Mr. Haraqija had?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I was not in their table. I was sitting at another table.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, does that mean you were not able to hear all of the conversations that Mr. Haraqija engaged in that evening after the theatre in this restaurant in D6?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to hear everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No re-examination. Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that Mr. Haraqija and Mr. Morina worked in the same office in the Ministry of Culture and Sport and Youth?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: They didn't work in the same office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, in the same ministry.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, in the same ministry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you were not always with them on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No, only with Mr. Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that they could have met in the ministry without you being there?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: The office of Mr. Haraqija was on the other side and Mr. Morina's on the opposite side of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not my question. Will you please answer my question. Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that possibility does exist, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were not always with Mr. Haraqija; you were only with him at those times when you were driving him out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, I can make that concession as well. I can make these concessions. He's not a bed-fellow of the client; and, of course, it's open that meetings could have taken place in the ministry. A concession can be made, Your Honours, by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just trying to find out what the relevance of this whole study of the cafe you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll address that in closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no further questions, Mr. Khan, may I take it that the questions of the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm most grateful. Perhaps the witness can be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kuqi, this concludes your testimony. I thank you for having come and having answered the questions. Mr. Khan, I think that the 92 ter statement has not been assigned a number yet. Of course, you made the application to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... but, nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it can be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number D7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D7. I think we decided already that it was admitted as --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... under the condition that the condition has been fulfilled. So, therefore, D7 is in now evidence. The witness may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful. Whilst the usher -- and perhaps, as you know, the next witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very, very sorry to interrupt my learned friend. There is just one point that I must communicate to the Trial Chamber because I gave some incorrect information to the Trial Chamber a few moments ago, and I need to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the conversation whether -- there was discussion about whether Mr. Haraqija had seen a particular document or not, and I informed the Chamber and the parties that this document formed part of the confirmation material for this case which would have been then disclosed at the initial appearance. And I believed that to be the case because my staff provided me with such a binder in which this document is present; however, my case manager has informed me that this particular document was not part of the confirmation materials that were filed with this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to have that on the record. I think the Chamber expressed itself already about how important it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm not intending to call the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Agim Kasapolli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I should resign and retire. I am an abysmal failure in giving time estimates. I was very much hopeful we would finish today, but matters have dragged on. I think I'll be -- he's also giving some evidence as to the character of the accused. So perhaps less than half an hour, 20 minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I'm -- how long would you like me to spend with this witness? I'm trying to be as helpful as possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is still very much inclined to see whether we can finish today. I do understand that we could continue until 2.00. We'll be a bit more strict now on times. We'll first have the break. The break will be until 20 minutes to 1.00. Then, Mr. Khan, if it will be possible for you to examine the witness in 20 minutes or less, would that be feasible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as long as my learned friend doesn't mind me leading on some matters, I'll try to be as judicious as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you, Mr. Saxon, be very organized in your cross-examination, so that we could finish by five minutes past 1.00. Mr. Dieckmann, do you have any questions for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to indicate that there could be a very few numbers of questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see whether we can then finish not later than ten minutes past 1.00, then we'd have another 50 minutes. The parties are invited to see whether they can be so focused in their closing argument. I think that most of the issues are perfectly clear to the Chamber. So, therefore, there's no need in any way to repeat anything which we find already in the pre-trial briefs. Of course, the Chamber's carefully listened to the testimony of today and has not found many new issues. The parties are invited to consider that. Mr. Saxon, would you think that that would be possible, 50 minutes -- well, let's say, would it be fair to say 20 minutes for the Prosecution and each Defence team 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Absolutely impossible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no closing brief. I've really bent over backwards, I think in fairness, to be as efficient as I can with the use of time. I didn't expect the last witness even would take ever so long. I've tried to make concessions wherever I can; but on some issues, I must dig in. I think -- my inclination for the Trial Chamber's knowledge is that I was expecting and I was going to ask for an hour and a half for closing speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said an hour to match Mr. Saxon, and I will try to do it within half an hour or thereabouts, but 15 minutes is impossible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the further scheduling during the break. We will also take into consideration how the time is used. Until now - and I'm not saying this party or that party - but in total we have not worked as efficiently as we could have worked. I leave it to that. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: One additional matter for saving time, there are two 92 bis statements. I'm in Your Honours' hands. Perhaps there's no need to read them out in totality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that under the present circumstances, the 92 bis statements could just be assigned numbers and that we do not have any urgent need to have them summarized and read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I take it you'll be Mr. Kasapolli?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I do understand that -- I do learn that you can hear me in a language you understand. Mr. Kasapolli, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration. The text will now be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kasapolli. You'll first be examined by Mr. Khan who is counsel for Mr. Haraqija. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, perhaps we can go into private session for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Monkhouse.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Your name, again, is Agim Kasapolli?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And, in 2007, you were the advisor to one of the ministers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And which minister was that?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: In the Ministry of Culture, Youth, and Sport, I was the advisor for sport.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the name of the incumbent minister?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Mr. Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now you're a journalist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a journalist.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you've been a journalist since January the 9th, 2008?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You're well-known in Kosova; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've been a TV commentator for the last eight Olympic games, is that correct, on Pristina television?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, on Pristina television. Now it's Kosova television.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you also write articles for the Bota Sot newspaper at the moment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And you get paid per article whenever you submit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I write for other newspapers, too, not only for Bota Sot, but yes is my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember the opening of a theatre in Peja in 2007?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you attend that function?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you tell Their Honours the date of that function.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: 2nd July 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How did you get to that function?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Together with the minister and a driver, we were in a jeep and headed directly to Peja.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And the name of the driver that you travelled with?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, but he was a driver from another ministry.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Bajrush Morina go to that event?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: He did participate, he went to the event, but he was not in the jeep with me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How did he get there, do you know?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Bajrush was in another vehicle together with Veli Bytyqi, while myself and the minister and a driver were in a jeep, in a different vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And if you can just address your answers to Their Honours, I'd appreciate it. Now, sir, before the theatre, did you go straight into the theatre or did you have an interlude before you entered those premises?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Before we went to the theatre, we were in the Metohija Hotel and had a drink there; before we went to the theatre, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you stand or did you sit?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Some were standing and some others were sitting. A considerable number of people were there, that's why some were standing and some were seated.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What about you, were you standing or were you seated?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I was seated next to the minister.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And who was on the other side of the minister, if anybody?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: On the other side of the minister was his wife.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you describe very briefly the atmosphere whilst you had that coffee?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Some people were standing, as I already said, while the minister was in the middle. I don't remember exactly whether his wife was on his left or right, but I was seated next to him. We discussed the opening of the theatre, of the piece that was supposed to be played in the theatre that night.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And then you went into the theatre, is that correct, after the coffee?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No. We waited, standing in front of the theatre. There were many guests coming, and there, too, we discussed the play that was supposed to start any minute then.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During that period of time, as you were going into the theatre, were you with the minister or away from the minister, Haraqija?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I was with the minister.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And after the theatre opening, did you go home or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: When the play finished, we went to a dinner organized by the host in Peja, by the director of the theatre. He organized a solemn dinner attended by a large number of people, even larger than that of those standing in front of the theatre.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where were you sitting at the dinner in relation to Mr. Haraqija?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Again, I was seated next to the minister. He was in the middle and on his other side was his wife. So we were seated in a row, meaning I was the first, minister was in the middle, and on the other side was his wife.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And, again, during this dinner afterwards, could you very briefly in a couple of sentences describe the atmosphere of the dinner?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very pleasant, cozy atmosphere. The play at that night was quite interesting. We commented on the actors. The minister was quite satisfied with the theatre opening and the play itself. I wasn't. Many other guests, including the director, engaged in the conversation; and, overall, they had a positive impression of the play played at the opening.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During the whole time on that day, before you entered the theatre, when you were in the theatre, and at the dinner afterwards, did you at any time hear anybody discuss the Haradinaj case and the Yugoslav Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anybody, and in particular the minister, Haraqija, discuss the protected witness that we've spoken about?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Minister Haraqija or anybody else speak about sending Mr. Morina to a third country?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I didn't even see Morina there by.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again briefly, because Their Honours need to have as much information as possible in a very tight time constraints, could you tell Their Honours very briefly what kind of man would you say Mr. Haraqija is? And let me say, firstly, professionally what kind of man would you say he is?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I was born in 1945, which means I am twice the age of Mr. Haraqija, Minister Haraqija. I was impressed by his decisiveness, commitment in work, and his high professionalism demonstrated during his work in the ministry. There were times when I disagreed with some issues surrounding sports; however, our cooperation was great. Of the age that he is, I think that there is a perspective for him because during the time we worked together, he demonstrated exceptional professionalism.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The Prosecution may ask you more questions about that. I have to move on, I only have a few minutes. But, personally, how would you describe what kind of man Astrit Haraqija is? And, perhaps, if you can give one or two examples, that would be of assistance to Their Honours in assessing the kind of man he is.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: As far as Haraqija as a person is concerned, I can say that during my time at work with Mr. Haraqija, he is a humane person. Concretely, when a policeman had his father sick and in danger but had no means to support the health care of his father, I was pleasantly surprised because the economic situation, as you know, in Kosova is very poor, Astrit Haraqija contributed with half of his personal salary to the curing of this person. Second example that really touched me was when Mr. Haraqija showed a respect towards the ministry -- minister who was suffering from cancer. He found the adequate ways to substitute for her work, supported her materially and morally for her to overcome this illness. Finally, this young man, when this female minister died, he was on an official trip, and he found the time to speak on the phone with me and to instruct me on how to organize her funeral. We did this in accordance with the means in our disposal. The third example, and I will mention only these three because there are many examples of this kind, is when a well-known actor in Kosova, Hadi Shehu - maybe the best actor in Kosova, who dedicated his entire life to arts - was ill, since the ministry has quite small funds and cannot help people, due to the authority of Mr. Haraqija, we managed to raise funds to secure a kidney transplant for this person in Moscow. He lives and he is well due to the humanity and good deeds of Mr. Haraqija. As I said, I can single out many other examples, but these are the three concrete ones that I can say right now.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm grateful, sir, and you've been admirably short. If you can stay there, there will some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, out of time, I'm not putting the -- I've got blank photographs of the same nature that I was shown previously that I was going to put to the witness. Mr. Saxon is welcome to have them should he wish clarification, but I'm not going to spend time on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Dieckmann, who's counsel for Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Jens Dieckmann. I have just a few numbers of question. You know Mr. Bajrush Morina, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You know him being a political journalist for the Bota Sot?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: As a former editor-in-chief of Bota Sot?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you know him being the former editor-in-chief of the Bota Sot?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you have been able to read his articles during the last years in the Bota Sot?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Of course, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You agree with me that he is a professional political journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Bajrush Morina has always been a supporter of the former President Rugova and his party; true?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And as far as you know, he was never a member of the party of Ramush Haradinaj; is it true, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No. He never was a member of his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And as a journalist, he has frequently written critical articles against Ramush Haradinaj and his party; true?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. Not only for his party, he wrote critical reviews even for Rugova when he thought that that should be done; in other words, this demonstrates his professionalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So you know him as a good person, a person with a good character; would you say this?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. Mr. Saxon, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Saxon who is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Kasapolli, I'd like to ask you to turn your mind to the drink that you and the other persons had at the -- I believe it's the cafe or restaurant Metohija before the -- before the theatre on the 2nd of July, all right? You mentioned that there were a number of people there, and so some people had to stand. So there was a lot of noise in the room, wasn't there, people talking?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the same would actually be true for the dinner that took place after the theatre because there were actually many more people present, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: But there was an order there, the minister greeted all those present, and all took the floor in sequence, in turns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And the minister greeted everyone who was present, right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: He greeted the director first of the play and then the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the minister greet everyone who was present in that room for that dinner; that's my question?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So that means that the minister at least at one point would have greeted Mr. Morina, right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, why do you say no to my last question when previously you said that the minister greeted everyone -- Mr. Kasapolli, you need to let me finish my question, okay? Why do you say no to my last question when previously you said that the minister greeted everyone there in the room?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: May I give you my answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I said already that the minister greeted the director of the play and the others. In the area where I was seated, next to the minister, and where his wife was sitting, we were not able to see Bajrush Morina. Perhaps he was further away because there were many tables. And it is quite natural if you greet everyone, and if Bajrush happened to be there, he would have greeted him, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So just so that the record is clear, it's your testimony that Mr. Morina was seated a long distance away from Mr. Haraqija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No, no. This is not what I said. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fairness, the witness was very clear at the outset. He said he didn't even know if Bajrush Morina was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said that about the dinner, Mr. Khan, and not about the first meeting. You asked him this question in the context of who was at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- dinner. Mr. Saxon, I don't know whether the witness knows, which apparently is included in your question, that Mr. Morina was seated. Perhaps we could first clarify that. Do you remember whether Mr. Morina, when having drinks before going to the theatre, whether Mr. Morina was seated?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour. I'm very, very sorry. We were still talking now, though, about the dinner which was after the theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check, yes. Let me just check if you're right. I apologise, Mr. Saxon. Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I asked, this is at line 21 of page 82: "Did the minister greet everyone who was present in that room for that dinner; that's my question?" "Yes, of course." Then the questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Then I missed that portion. I apologise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Kasapolli, you said that: "At that dinner, I believe we didn't even see Bajrush." And if that's the case, then, Bajrush was seated nowhere near you, nowhere near the minister; right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I will repeat it again. When the opening ended, everybody went to the solemn dinner. The number compared to the people who were at the hotel before the theatre was four-fold higher. So the opening was over, we went together to the dinner, the number of people was huge. I did not say that he was or he wasn't there, but I -- he was not in the area where I was sitting with the minister. I didn't see him that night because it was very crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. At that dinner, I know that the minister was sitting to one side of you. Who was sitting on your other side?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: You mean sitting opposite to me or next to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Next to you on the other side.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: So it was me, the minister, his wife, there were also some actors who participated in the play, and the director was about four chairs away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Kasapolli, was there anyone seated on your other side?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Of course, there was someone else seated on my side because all the tables were full.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you spoke to that person at some point during the dinner, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I spoke with the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you saying that you completely ignored the person on your other side during that entire dinner? You never spoke to that person?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: We had everyday conversation there. I don't remember everyone I spoke with. We mainly discussed the opening, the theatre, the play. I didn't even congratulate the director on the play because I didn't like it; but as I said earlier, the minister quite liked it and conveyed his congratulations to the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony then, there were at least some moments when you did not focus on what the minister was doing or saying; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: As far as I know, when people go to a dinner, they consider this dinner as a relaxation. At all times I was at the disposal of the minister as his counsellor, advisor. So, since the topic was the theatre, the conversation was mainly about the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand my last question? Should I repeat it again?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I understood your question and I responded to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasapolli, whether you responded to the question is still to be seen. Mr. Saxon asked you whether you had conversation with the person sitting at the other side, not the minister but the person sitting at the other side. Did he understand your testimony well that you had conversations with that other person as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that I spoke with someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking about someone else, but about the person sitting next to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't remember whether you had no conversation whatsoever with the person sitting next to you other than the minister who was sitting at the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, it was the director of the play that was played that night. On the opposite side, there was some actors sitting because they gathered around the minister, the actors and the director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the director of the play, you don't remember whether you exchanged any word with him that evening at dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We greeted each other because we come from the same town; we both come from Peja. We greeted each other, we exchanged some words, I said to him that I didn't like the play. So this was a conversation I had with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question of Mr. Saxon was whether you would agree that if you have a conversation with someone else on, for example, whether you liked the play or not, whether you would agree that you could not at the same time focus on what Mr. Haraqija was doing and saying. Would you agree with Mr. Saxon on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one more question. Mr. Kasapolli, if you are engaged with -- if you were engaged in conversation with the director of the play, how could you have then heard at that moment what Mr. Haraqija was discussing, if anything?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a request. I did not say that I was -- could speak to one person to the director and at the same time hear the minister. We were sitting at a table. We had normal, civilised conduct with people, talking to people. When you finish talking to one person, you turn to the other person if he asks you something. You can't speak to two people on two sides at the same time, with a minister at one side and someone else at the other side at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that explanation, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one or more questions for you, Mr. Kasapolli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take you back to having drinks before you went to the theatre. You told us that some people were standing, some people were seated. At that time, during drinks, did you see Mr. Morina?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you were seated. Were you seated in the group?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No. I was with the minister and with his -- a woman from Gjakova because the minister's chauffeur had gone to Gjakova to get someone and take them to Peja. And when the minister's wife arrived, we were sitting, the minister and then me and his wife. Like everywhere else where we sat, we were together. Then those people were interested in the play. The director and everyone else, they came and arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking about the subject of your conversation at that moment. Now, were you seated around a table?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: There were several tables, two or three tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were seated around these tables; is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means tables put together and the people seated around the, as you said, two or three tables?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Yes. And there were other people who were standing, because all these seats were taken and the rest of the people had to stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this group seated around the two or three tables, was Mr. Morina in that group seated around these two or three tables?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you didn't see him there. Do you consider it possible that he would have been seated within a distance of, let's say, three to four metres from you, or do you consider this not a possibility?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I can't say anything about it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kasapolli, let me explain to you. If I'm in a room with other people, there's hardly any chance that I'll miss the person sitting next to me or to the other side or at close range, but there might be someone further away. I ask you whether, going back in your memory and the situation, whether you might have missed Mr. Morina as being seated within three or four metres from you.

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I know Mr. Morina as a colleague from the ministry, but on that day there were a lot of people there. And having set out from Pristina at the end of the day, if I'd seen him, I would have remembered him, but I don't remember seeing him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I'm asking you - where you say who was sitting next to you, who was sitting next to that person, being the wife of the minister - whether you would have missed Mr. Morina within a distance of three or four metres from you, or do you say he wasn't that close to me, he may have been further away, I might have missed him. What's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I just didn't see him there. I can't speculate. I can't say that -- something that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see all the people that were seated around those tables?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: No. I was concentrating on the minister and his wife and a couple of people from Peja who were near me. I wasn't interested in everyone else who was in the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many people approximately were seated around these tables? Was it five, ten, 20?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: I don't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid there is, just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: When you say, sir, that Mr. Haraqija greeted all those present, what do you mean by "greeted"? Can you tell exactly -- can you tell the Court exactly what Mr. Haraqija did to greet the people present?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That question presupposes that Mr. Kasapolli observed every single greeting and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if my friend will bear with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- if my friend will just trust me and bear with me for a moment, it may become clear; if not, I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what you meant by that. What did he do?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Haraqija was the minister for culture, sports, and youth. When the premier was over, we went to a common dinner, as I said; and when I say "he greeted," I mean that he congratulated those participants on the performance. He congratulated the theatre group on their performance that evening, as every minister would do after a performance at the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You must think I'm very slow. How did he congratulate them? Actually, what did he do? How did he convey his congratulations?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Well, he greeted everyone who was there and then he congratulated them on their success, the fact that in a short period of time the theatre in Peja had managed to put on such a good performance, discussed the financial problems that they had had and discussed the performance and with very modest means -- that it was carried out with modest means from the ministry. He discussed this and just said that we had had a great success that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: When he discussed this, was it to individuals or to the group as a whole? Was it to everybody present or was it individuals?

utterances.speaker: EDMOND KUQI
utterances.text: Everyone was present and the minister was standing in their midst, and so it was a collective greeting, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, I hope that's clear. I have no further re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Has the further examination triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And neither the questions by the Bench, then, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes your evidence, Mr. Kasapolli. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to this court and having answered all the questions by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. And whilst the witness is being escorted out, I wonder if the Registry have managed to assign numbers for the 92 bis statement of Zana Haraqija and also Zija Rugova, so they can be part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 92 bis packet of Haraqija will be Exhibit D8; and the 92 bis packet for Rugova becomes Exhibit Number D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D8 and 9, they were admitted already in evidence, but they were not assigned numbers yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Monkhouse and Your Honour. Your Honour, that is the case for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, first of all, Mr. Dieckmann, we understood from Mr. Khan that he's closed his case. Is the same true for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We do not intend to present any witness or any additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm inquiring whether we could continue until 2.00 today, because under those circumstances I would invite you, Mr. Saxon, to make your closing argument in the next half an hour. The Chamber has some difficulties tomorrow to start early due to private reasons which are beyond the control of the Chamber. So, therefore, the Chamber would like to finish, conclude the case, in the latter half of the morning session, that would be to start either at 11.30 or 12.00. We would then have still one hour and a half approximately. If you would give your closing argument today, Mr. Saxon, then tomorrow time would be there for the Defence teams to give their closing argument and there would be still time, little time, for any further questions by the Bench and any further responses to what the other party has presented in his closing argument. Yes. Mr. Saxon, we have time until 2.00. That would mean that you would have half an hour. I'll give same time to Defence tomorrow. Could you present your closing argument. And there's one issue which I have to ask. To what extent does it bother you that you have not yet finally decided on the admission of the statements, the one by Mr. Schook and the other by a 92 ter witness? If that would influence your closing argument, then, of course, we would have to find a solution for that first. The Chamber wanted, as a matter of fact, to further consider this matter this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, any influence on the Prosecution's closing argument would be quite minor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having said this, are you confident to then give your closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have half an hour, and it's not only my authority but any later will be a problem is on my little paper which is in front of me. Please present your closing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence that you have heard in this trial proves beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Morina, Bajrush Morina, interfered with Witness 2 by trying to convince him to change or withdraw his testimony against Ramush Haradinaj. And I would simply direct your attention, Your Honour, to the following portions of Exhibit P12, which was the recording of the first meeting, page 17, lines 13 to 22 in the English version; page 17, lines 33, to page 18, line 8 in the Albanian version; page 21, lines 22 to 30 in the English version; page 22, lines 14 to 22 in the Albanian version; as well as in the English version page 22, line 24 to page 23, line 11; and in the Albanian version, page 23, line 15, to page 24, line 3. I would also direct the Chamber's attention to what is now Exhibit P19 which was the Prosecution's interview with Mr. Morina on the 26th of October, 2007, at page 28, lines 23 to 30, the English version; page 25, lines 6 to 17 in the Albanian version, Mr. Morina explains that Mr. Haraqija instructed Mr. Morina to go see Witness 2 and ask him not to give evidence. I would also briefly direct your attention to the two statements of Witness 2, Exhibits P7 and P8; and the SMS messages from Mr. Morina to Witness 2, which is Exhibit P4; as well as the testimony of Witness Number 1. Moving, Your Honour, to the question of the criminal responsibility of Mr. Haraqija. Your Honours, you have heard evidence in this trial that Mr. Morina supports a wife, several children, elderly parents on approximately -- excuse me, at least at the time of these events, Mr. Morina supported his family on a salary of approximately 400 Euros per month. This is at page 166 of the transcript. He and his family rent an apartment in Pristina. Due to these circumstances, Mr. Morina acknowledged to Witness 2 that sometimes he was in a bad position. And this is in Exhibit P12 in the English translation page 9, lines 1 to 9; and in the Albanian transcript, page 9, lines 4 to 12. Your Honours, the Defence position is that Mr. Haraqija did not direct Mr. Morina to meet with Witness 2 in order to convince Witness 2 to change or withdraw his testimony, nor that Mr. Haraqija had anything to do with the events in this case. Your Honours, if you are going to accept that proposition, then, respectfully, you must also accept, at a minimum, the following points: That Bajrush Morina, a man of such humble means, independently would take it upon himself to, first, participate in what his immediate supervisor, Angjelina Krasniqi, agreed was an "abuse of office" to use the public funds of the Ministry of Culture allegedly for personal reasons, to travel to the third country to meet with a protected witness in a notorious trial, to discuss a newspaper article written five years before. And that reference to abuse of office can be found in Exhibit P11, Prosecution interview with Ms. Krasniqi on the 7th of November, 2007, page 5, lines 20 to 31 in the English; page 7, lines 12 to 25 in the Albanian.
